1. Introduction 
 
The fourth industrial revolution has brought about substantial transformations in the implementation of cloud 
computing platforms aimed at improving service delivery in the public sector. These systems enable the transfer of information 
in a clear and easily accessible way while also reducing inefficiency and fostering collaboration within organizations 
(Majstorovic et al., 2020). Cloud computing enhances efficiency, fosters research and development, and stimulates economic 
growth (Srivastava and Řežábek, 2022). The potential advantages of such platforms have motivated numerous governments 
worldwide to embrace various platforms aimed at improving service delivery and accountability. 
Government institutions are showing a growing dedication to investing in digital projects, which is part of a larger trend 
of increasing spending on information technology to replace outmoded systems. The findings of Gartner's 2023 CIO and 
Technology Executive Survey from 81 countries revealed that 57% of government finance officers intend to allocate more funds 
toward the enhancement of application modernization (Gartner, 2023). The commitment to improve accountability through 
enhanced platforms cuts across various sectors, including financial management in the public sector, due to the scarcity of 
financial resources. The need to move away from inefficient manual processes necessitated development partners such as the 
World Bank to invest large sums of dollars in the deployment of integrated financial management information systems (IFMIS) 
across various countries (Dener, 2024). This technological advancement allows for faster transaction processing, a reduction 
in inefficiencies commonly caused by human errors, and significant financial savings (Oduro et al., 2022; Hashim and Piatti-
Fünfkirchen, 2018; Dener, 2024; Entsie et al., 2024). 
The execution of e-government cloud efforts is significantly challenging, notwithstanding the influence of national 
legislation (Liang et al., 2017). The presence of these impediments affects the efficient implementation of cloud computing in 
government environments, causing concerns about the preparedness of public sector organizations to adopt cloud

Abstract Developing economies are faced with difficulties in providing efficient public services to satisfy the increasing 
demands of citizens amidst diminishing public resources and funding. Although there are empirical evidence by researchers 
on the benefical impact of the utilization of cloud services, the deployment is often faced with challenges. The existence of 
these obstacles hinders the effective deployment of cloud computing in governmental settings, raising concerns regarding 
factors which assist public sector organizations to embrace cloud technologies. Despite findings from previous studies, the 
role top management support (TMS) in the adoption of cloud computing in the public sector in Ghana remains 
underexplored. This study aims to provide insights into potential factors that could influence cloud computing adoption 
decisions in the public sector within the Ghanaian context under the mediating role of TMS. This study examines factors of 
adoption using a sample size of 175 participants. The research employs a modified Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory to 
assess the mediating role of TMS in impacting factors namely, relative advantage, complexity and government policy. The 
findings indicate that relative advantage and government policy impact on the adoption with TMS acting as a mediator 
between these parameters and adoption. Surprisingly, it was discovered that complexity did not have a significant effect on 
adoption under the mediating role of TMS. These findings emphasize the significance of government support, reletive 
advantage and TMS in promoting the implementation. Although the study successfully achieved its goals, it is important to 
note that there were some limitations. This study enhances the existing body of knowledge by presenting emperical basis 
on the influence of TMS on the adoption of GIFMIS. It also provides practical guidance for policymakers and administrators 
who aim to enhance financial management in the public sector. 
 
Keywords: public financial management, diffusion of Innovation, cloud computing, top management support

2. Literature Review 
 
The Ghana Integrated Financial Management Information System (GIFMIS) is a customized version of the IFMIS, 
specifically for Ghana. It was launched in May 2014, succeeding in the Budget and Public Expenditure Management System 
Project, which functioned from 1999-2008. GIFMIS was established to consolidate the collection and organization of financial 
data, thereby enhancing budget planning, execution, and financial reporting (Ghana Budget Statement, 2014). Envisioned as a 
component of the e-Ghana Project, it was designed to be funded through consolidated donor and country resources. GIFMIS 
functions as an instrument for treasury management, budget formulation, financial oversight, and the conversion of essential 
financial data into information required by decision-makers (Hashim and Piatti-Fünfkirchen, 2018). 
 
2.1. Theoretical Background 
 
 
Researchers have employed different theoretical frameworks to elucidate the choice to embrace technology, such as 
the resource-based view (RBV) theory (Abdussalaam et al., 2020), the technology acceptance model (TAM) (Oduro et al., 2022), 
the diffusion of innovations (DOI) model (Sun et al., 2018), the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) 
(Shahzad et al., 2022), the technology organization environment (TOE) framework (Amini & Javid, 2023) and the theory of 
planned behavior (TPB) (Al-Mawali et al., 2022). 
In a systematic analysis of theories, Zamani (2022) identified DOI as one of the main theories used by researchers in 
studies on the adoption of technologies. This study used DOI theory in line with prior research by Ashogbon and Markham 
(2023) and Shaikh et al. (2023). They emphasized that DOI is a crucial model for ensuring seamless integration of cloud 
computing by successfully reducing risks and improving the understanding of implementation variables. Some researchers have 
also extended DOI theory to enhance its application (Ramayah et al., 2013; Shaikh et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024; Alyoubi & 
Yamin, 2021). 
 
3. Hypotheses 
 
3.1. Complexity and the Adoption of GIFMIS 
 
 
Complexity has been identified as a significant barrier to the adoption of cloud computing systems. The concept of 
complexity refers to the degree to which an innovation is perceived as difficult to understand and use (Rogers, 1983). High 
complexity can deter potential adopters due to the anticipated challenges associated with the implementation and operation 
of new systems. Studies have shown the negative effects of complexity on the adoption of various technologies, such as cloud 
computing (Amini and Javid, 2023), artificial intelligent technology (Chen et al., 2021), blockchain (Choi et al., 2020; Wong et 
al., 2020), and big data (Lutfi et al., 2022). Furthermore, other studies have shown that higher levels of perceived complexity 
can lead to resistance from users, thereby hindering the successful adoption of such systems (Maroufkhani et al., 2022; Ali et 
al., 2020; Marei et al., 2021). Therefore, the following hypothesis is proposed: 
H1: Complexity will negatively impact the adoption of the GFMIS. 
 
3.2. Relative advantages and GIFMIS 
 
Relative advantage refers to the degree to which a new technology is perceived as better than the existing solutions. 
When top management recognizes the benefits of adopting cloud computing technologies, such as improved efficiency, 
enhanced financial control, and better decision-making capabilities, they are more likely to support their implementation.

Empirical studies posit a positive relationship between perceived relative advantage and technology adoption. For instance, Ali 
et al. (2020) emphasized that the perceived benefits and improvements brought by cloud computing technology significantly 
influence its adoption by local government institutions. Furthermore, various studies have indicated that cloud computing 
technology reduces costs, saves business time, enhances sales and productivity, and offers opportunities for the utilization of 
shared resources (Yuan et al., 2020; Dixit et al., 2021; Marei et al., 2021). Therefore, the following hypothesis is proposed: 
H2: Relative advantage significantly impacts the adoption of GIFMIS. 
 
3.3. Government Policy and GIFMIS 
 
The adoption of cloud technology could be influenced by regulations, compliance requirements, and policies from 
various sectors. These compliance factors can either support or impede the implementation of cloud technology, as they play 
a significant role in establishing the operational environment for institutions. Lynn et al. (2020) highlighted the importance of 
government policy in the adoption of cloud computing, specifically in high-performance computing sectors. Prior researchers 
have underscored the importance of government policies leading to the adoption of such platforms (Marei et al., 2021; Wang 
et al., 2018; Ali & Valmira 2020). Therefore, we propose the following: 
H3: Government policy will have a significant positive effect on the adoption of GIFMIS. 
 
3.4. Complexity and Top Management Support 
 
Complexity can act as a significant barrier discouraging top managers from endorsing and facilitating the 
implementation of advanced systems. Mohammed et al. (2023) highlighted that the complexity of a Cloud-based ERP System 
hampers its diffusion, as organizations are reluctant to adopt technologies perceived as overly complex. This reluctance is 
echoed by Maroufkhani et al. (2022), who noted that managers are less inclined to support the adoption of big data analytics 
if they believe it entails substantial effort. Furthermore, authors such as Oliviera et al. (2014) and Sharma et al. (2021) argued 
that the complexity of a technology significantly influences management's adoption decisions. On the basis of prior studies, 
the following conclusions are proposed: 
H4: Complexity significantly impacts top management support. 
 
3.5. Relative advantages and top management support 
 
When top management perceives that adopting a cloud platform offers significant benefits such as increased efficiency, 
better financial oversight, and enhanced decision-making capabilities, their support for its implementation is likely to increase. 
Chienwattanasook et al. (2021) highlighted that perceived relative advantage significantly impacts top management's 
endorsement of cloud computing adoption in universities, as the clear benefits motivate leaders to champion its 
implementation. Researchers have demonstrated that leaders are more inclined to adopt cloud computing when they 
recognize its advantages over traditional systems (Ali et al., 2020; Daoud et al., 2021). Therefore, the following hypothesis is 
proposed: 
H5: Relative advantage significantly impacts top management support in the adoption of GIFMIS. 
 
3.6. Government Support and Top Management Support 
 
The role of government initiatives in enabling or obstructing the technology adoption process is crucial, indicating that 
effective policies are vital for promoting technology integration (Raut et al., 2019; Shirpoor 2023; Mudawi et al., 2023). 
Government policies affect the views and decision-making of managers in regard to cloud computing (Yigitbasioglu, 2015; 
Mudawi et al. 2023). These observations emphasize the importance of establishing a legal framework that fosters trust in cloud 
technologies, especially in public sector organizations and e-government systems, to encourage technical progress and improve 
organizational effectiveness. We therefore hypothesize the following: 
H6: Government support positively influences top management support in the adoption of GIFMIS. 
 
3.7. Top Management Support and GIFMIS 
 
Empirical studies emphasize the critical role of senior management support in influencing the adoption of cloud 
computing. The successful adoption of cloud technology is typically dependent on the commitment of senior management 
since it offers strategic guidance and allocates resources (Alshamaila et al., 2013; Hadwer et al., 2021; Low et al., 2011; Daoud 
et al., 2021). In addition, leaders can actively promote the use of cloud computing to address obstacles such as cost concerns 
and technological complexity, hence ensuring a more seamless implementation process (Alshamaila et al., 2013). This 
assistance is especially crucial in influencing the perceived benefits of cloud technology and improving the preparedness of 
organizations for digital transformation. We therefore propose the following: 
H7: Top management support positively influences the adoption of GIFMIS.

Complexity is a critical factor that influences the perception and decision-making processes of top management 
regarding the adoption of new technologies. High levels of perceived complexity can lead to negative perceptions among top 
managers, ultimately hindering their intention to support and adopt such technologies. Studies have shown that complexity 
negatively impacts the adoption of big data analytics (BDA), as evidenced by the works of Maroufkhani et al. (2022) and Lutfi 
et al. (2022), computer-assisted auditing techniques by Daoud et al. (2021) and electronic procurement by Marei et al. (2021). 
Moreover, empirical research shows that senior management support plays a crucial role in connecting the relationship 
between relative advantage and the adoption of cloud computing. Compared with current systems, the concept of relative 
advantage, which refers to the perceived benefits and enhancements that cloud computing provides, has constantly been 
recognized as a significant factor influencing decisions to embrace cloud computing (Rogers, 2003; Salah et al., 2021; Oliveira 
et al., 2014; Marei et al., 2021; Chienwattanasook et al., 2021). 
Furthermore, studies indicate that the backing of top-level executives is crucial in facilitating the connection between 
government policy and the use of cloud computing. Government policies, including those pertaining to data security, privacy 
legislation, and financial incentives, play a crucial role in driving the adoption of cloud technology across different sectors 
(Oliveira et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018). The findings of previous studies lead to the formulation of the following hypotheses: 
H8a: The TMS mediates the relationship between complexity and the adoption of GIFMIS. 
H8b: The TMS mediates the relationship between relative advantage and the adoption of GIFMIS. 
H8c: The TMS mediates the relationship between government policy and the adoption of GIFMIS.

4. Materials and methods 
 
The study employs a cross-sectional survey design. A cross-sectional survey methodology allows for the collection of 
data from a sample of respondents at a certain moment in time (Saunders et al., 2019). The survey design aligns with previous 
studies conducted by the authors investigating the factors influencing the adoption of ICT platforms, such as Salah et al. (2021). 
This approach is appropriate for this study since it allows for the examination of the factors that impact the adoption of cloud 
service platforms, such as GIFMIS. 
The population for this study comprises personnel of the Metropolitan, Municipal, and District Assemblies (MMDAs) in 
Ghana who utilize the GIFMIS platform. The Metropolitan, Municipal, and District Assemblies (MMDAs) are the local governing 
bodies responsible for implementing government policy. The MMDAs were selected as the research area because of their 
ability to represent the national government through local administrations. The researchers employed purposive sampling to 
select the participants, in accordance with previous studies conducted by Al-Okaily and Al-Okaily (2022) and Carsamer and 
Abbam (2020). 
 
4.1. Measurement instrument 
 
 
For our study, we utilized a two-section questionnaire to gather data from participants. The initial portion collected 
demographic data and general information pertaining to the utilization of the GIFMIS platform. Consistent with our research 
framework, the second portion included seven components, each of which was evaluated by multiple items. The items were 
obtained from prior studies but were adjusted to fit the GIFMIS scenario. The measurement of each construct was conducted 
via a 5-point Likert scale, which ranged from 1 (indicating severe disagreement) to 5 (indicating strong agreement). Five 
constructs, namely, ICT infrastructure, complexity, relative advantage, top management support and GIFMIS, were measured 
via Likert scales. The scales used in this study were derived from Alghushami et al. (2020) and Jayeola et al. (2022) on top 
management support, Awa et al. (2016) on ICT infrastructure, Moore & Benbasat (1991) on complexity and Huang et al. (2020), 
and Moore and Benbasat (1991) on relative advantage.

5.2.Measurement model assessment 
 
The measurement model was evaluated via key criteria such as individual item reliability, construct reliability,

composite reliability exceeded 0.702, indicating acceptable reliability, as supported by Barclay et al. (2016). Convergent validity 
was measured by calculating the average variance extracted (AVE), which represents the proportion of variance a construct 
captures from its items relative to variance due to measurement error. The results presented in Table 2 show AVE values 
ranging from 0.793 to 0.887, all of which are above the recommended minimum of 0.50 suggested by Hair et al. (2021), 
confirming the convergent validity of the measurement model. Details of the Cronbach’s alpha, composite reliability and 
average variance extracted for all the variables are shown in Table 2.

5.3. Structural model assessment 
 
The significance of the hypothesized relationships between the constructs was assessed via path coefficients, t statistics, 
and p values. Furthermore, the conceptual model was evaluated for its predictive performance by measuring the proportion 
of variation explained (R²) (Hair et al., 2021). To examine the structural model, bootstrapping was used with 10,000 replications, 
as described by Hair et al. (2021). Standard metrics used to assess structural models include the path coefficient, coefficient of 
determination (R²), and Q². In addition, the PLSpredict approach, which assesses the model's ability to make accurate 
predictions on out-of-sample data, was utilized (Shmueli et al., 2019). Consequently, these analyses were carried out within 
the context of the structural model in the next sections. 
The adjusted coefficient of determination is employed to assess the structural model since it quantifies the model's 
prediction accuracy of in-sample data. As shown in Figure 1, the adjusted R² values for the adoption of the GIFMIS and the 
influence of the TMS were 0.35 and 0.32, respectively. The adjusted R² value for the TMS indicates that 35% of the variation in 
the GIFMIS is substantially explained by the exogenous variables in the research model. Additionally, 32% of the variation in 
the mediator variable, TMS, is accounted for by the variations in the exogenous variables. The results indicate that the 
explanatory power of the TMS and GIFMIS constructs is moderate (Hair et al., 2021). 
With respect to the hypotheses, five direct hypotheses were established to investigate the relationships among the 
constructs. The findings presented in Table 5 reveal that five of the seven hypotheses (H3, H3, H5, H6) achieved statistical 
significance at the 0.05 level, with t values surpassing the essential value of 1.645 for a one-tailed test. However, the effects of 
complexity on top management and GIFMIS were found to be insignificant, which led to the rejection of hypotheses H1 and 
H7, respectively. Table 5 shows details of the direct hypotheses.

6. Discussion 
 
The empirical findings suggest that both relative advantage and government policy have a significant positive influence 
on the adoption of GIFMIS. These results are in line with those of prior studies (Wang et al., 2018; Raut et al., 2019; Mudawi et 
al., 2023). These variables are also partially mediated by the TMS. Nevertheless, contrary to previous studies, this study 
revealed that complexity had no significant effect on the adoption of GIFMIS and was not mediated by the TMS (Maroufkhani 
et al., 2021; Oliviera et al., 2014; Marei et al., 2021). Consequently, our research reveals three crucial observations. 
First, government policies can directly facilitate organisations to use GIFMIS to maintain compliance by setting 
standards, guidelines, and compliance requirements. These rules might indirectly motivate senior management to promote 
cloud adoption by highlighting the strategic significance of harmonizing with legal frameworks, thus strengthening the role of 
the TMS in supporting cloud absorption. This underscores the importance of having regulatory environments that are 
supportive of promoting technological innovation and integration within organizations (Lynn et al, 2020; Wang et al., 2018). 
The indirect effect facilitated by top management support emphasizes the interaction between regulatory frameworks and 
organizational leadership in promoting the adoption of cloud computing which is in line with Wang et al. (2018). Government 
rules that emphasize the importance of cloud adoption are likely to help top management acknowledge the strategic value of 
GIFMIS and prioritize it. The role of the TMS in mediating highlights the significance of organizational leadership. 
Second, with respect to relative advantage, the direct effect implies that organisations are more inclined to adopt cloud 
computing technologies without reservation when they perceive clear benefits, such as cost savings, scalability and better 
efficiency. The direct impact of relative advantage on GIFMIS is supported by prior research (Marei et al., 2021; 
Chienwattanasook et al., 2021). The notion of a relative advantage offers a convincing justification for decision-makers to

allocate resources to cloud solutions since the concrete advantages are in line with their goals. The significance of the TMS in 
achieving these benefits is further emphasized by the indirect impact, which is mediated by the TMS in tandem with earlier 
work by Chienwattanasook et al. (2021). When senior executives recognize the strategic advantages of GIFMIS, they are more 
inclined to contribute resources, cultivate a supportive organizational culture, and spearhead activities that promote the use 
of cloud technology. These findings emphasize that endorsement from top management plays a crucial role in facilitating the 
translation of these perceived benefits into practical implementation of GIFMIS within the organization. 
Third, the finding that the effect of complexity is not significant for the adoption of cloud computing, either directly or 
indirectly through top management support, contradicts the hypothesis. The result is in tandem with El-Haddadeh et al. (2021) 
with regards to the mediation role of top management but contradiction to earlier result in a study by Maroufkhani et al. 
(2022). This implies that organisations may not view complexity as a major obstacle to adopting GIFMIS, potentially because 
of developments in cloud technologies that make deployment easier or the presence of external experts and support. Another 
possibility is that senior executives do not perceive complexity as a significant issue because of their proficiency in handling 
intricate IT projects or their reliance on established industry standards and collaboration with cloud service providers. Further 
investigations should examine these alternative aspects to acquire more profound insights into the other determinants of 
GIFMIS in organizational contexts. 
 
7. Conclusions 
 
This study investigated the mediating function of top management support (TMS) in the adoption of cloud computing 
within Ghana's public sector, emphasising the relationships among relative advantage, complexity, government policy, and 
adoption outcomes. The results indicate that both relative advantage and government policy favourably affect adoption whiles 
complexity does not significantly impact it when mediated by TMS. This indicates that organisations are more inclined to use 
cloud computing when they recognise distinct advantages and when conducive policies exist; yet the perceived complexity of 
the technology does not inherently impede adoption if there is robust leadership commitment. 
Moreover, the findings validate that TMS is helpful in enhancing the influence of facilitating factors on cloud adoption. 
It specifically enhances the impact of relative advantage and government policy, serving as a conduit between these factors 
and adoption decisions. Nonetheless, TMS fails to alleviate the adverse effects of complexity, indicating that resolving 
technological challenges necessitates supplementary measures beyond managerial assistance. These findings underscore the 
necessity for public sector leaders to advocate for cloud initiatives while ensuring that government policies effectively facilitate 
digital transformation. 
 
8. Implications 
 
The primary contribution of this study is the advancement of the literature by exploring the mediating role of the TMS 
in the relationship between various factors and GIFMIS adoption. Despite extensive studies on the usage and effectiveness of 
cloud computing across different sectors, there has been a lack of in-depth research focused on creating an implementation 
framework that ensures the successful and efficient use of GIFMIS in the public sector. Grounded in DOI theory, this study 
identified critical factors influencing GIFMIS adoption and examined the mediating role of the TMS in this process. Theoritically, 
the findings contribute to the development of a new contextual framework that links GP and TMS to GIFMIS adoption, thereby 
expanding the DOI model by integrating these factors in the context of GIFMIS adoption in Ghana. 
Furthermore, the results of this study have important practical consequences for policymakers and administrators who 
are responsible for implementing the GIFMIS in Ghana. The importance of relative advantage and government policy in 
predicting the adoption of the GIFMIS highlights the necessity for policy makers to prioritize benefits, such as enhanced fiscal 
control and effectiveness, which may prompt stakeholders to be more willing to embrace the system. Moreover, the significant 
impact of government policy indicates that it is essential to implement strong and supporting regulations with incentives to 
promote the widespread use of GIFMIS. 
Finally, the significance of top management support in the relationship between relative advantage, government policy, 
and GIFMIS adoption emphasizes the crucial importance of leadership in the adoption process. To achieve successful 
deployment of GIFMIS, it is crucial for senior management to actively embrace and support the system. 
 
9. Limitations and future directions 
 
Although this study effectively fulfills its goals, it has certain shortcomings. Initially, the extended DOI model underwent 
specific testing in the context of GIFMIS adoption, focusing exclusively on MMDAs as the study area. Subsequent studies should 
investigate how top management support affects the implementation of different theories. Additionally, it would be beneficial 
to evaluate this model via data from other public sector industries. In addition, this study revealed the insigficance of 
complexity as a factor in the adoption of GIFMIS. Future research could further explore qualitatively how the complexity of 
technological plafforms affects their adoption.

Abstract: Developing economies are faced with difficulties in providing efficient public services to satisfy the increasing demands of citizens amidst diminishing public resources and funding. Although there are empirical evidence by researchers on the benefical impact of the utilization of cloud services, the deployment is often faced with challenges. The existence of these obstacles hinders the effective deployment of cloud computing in governmental settings, raising concerns regarding factors which assist public sector organizations to embrace cloud technologies. Despite findings from previous studies, the role top management support (TMS) in the adoption of cloud computing in the public sector in Ghana remains underexplored. This study aims to provide insights into potential factors that could influence cloud computing adoption decisions in the public sector within the Ghanaian context under the mediating role of TMS. This study examines factors of adoption using a sample size of 175 participants. The research employs a modified Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory to assess the mediating role of TMS in impacting factors namely, relative advantage, complexity and government policy. The findings indicate that relative advantage and government policy impact on the adoption with TMS acting as a mediator between these parameters and adoption. Surprisingly, it was discovered that complexity did not have a significant effect on adoption under the mediating role of TMS. These findings emphasize the significance of government support, reletive advantage and TMS in promoting the implementation. Although the study successfully achieved its goals, it is important to note that there were some limitations. This study enhances the existing body of knowledge by presenting emperical basis on the influence of TMS on the adoption of GIFMIS. It also provides practical guidance for policymakers and administrators who aim to enhance financial management in the public sector.
